lessons.title: Why we sample and what a seed lot is
lessons.html:
A small sample speaks for the whole lot

A laboratory can only test a few hundred grams of seed, yet the result is used to describe a lot that may weigh many tonnes. If the sample is not representative, the germination, purity and moisture results on the label will be wrong. Farmers who plant that seed, and the company that sold it, carry the cost. Correct sampling is therefore the first and most important step in seed quality control.

The seed lot

A seed lot is a specified quantity of seed of one cultivar, physically identifiable by a unique lot number, in which every part is as uniform as practically possible. The maximum size of a lot for each crop is set by the seed testing rules and certification scheme that apply to you; your quality manager will give you the limits. Before sampling, check that:

  • all containers carry the same lot number and are labelled;
  • the lot is complete, stacked so that every container can be reached;
  • there are no obvious differences between containers, such as colour, treatment, damage or wet bags. A lot that looks uneven (heterogeneous) must be reported and not sampled as one lot.

Rules that apply

Seed in South Africa is controlled under the Plant Improvement Act 53 of 1976 and its regulations, and seed testing follows internationally agreed methods, mainly the International Seed Testing Association (ISTA) rules. Official or certification samples must be drawn by an authorised sampler. Always follow the latest procedure issued by your laboratory or certifying body.

Sample names you must know

TermMeaning
Primary sampleA small portion taken from one point in the lot
Composite sampleAll primary samples from the lot combined
Submitted sampleThe sample sent to the laboratory, reduced from the composite if needed
Working sampleThe portion the laboratory takes from the submitted sample for a test

Each step must keep the sample representative. Mistakes made early cannot be fixed later in the laboratory.

lessons.title: Drawing primary samples
lessons.html:
Equipment and technique

Sampling tools

  • Stick or sleeve trier: a long double tube with openings. It is pushed into a bag diagonally with the openings closed, opened to let seed flow in, closed and withdrawn. Good for free-flowing seed such as maize, wheat, soybeans and sunflower.
  • Nobbe trier: a short pointed tube for sampling bags at different depths.
  • Hand sampling: used for chaffy or fluffy seed, such as many grass seeds, that does not flow into a trier. The hand is inserted with fingers closed, then the seed is grasped firmly.
  • Automatic samplers: take portions from a moving seed stream during processing at regular intervals.

Clean every tool before you start and between lots, so seed from one lot cannot get into the next.

How many and where

The number of primary samples depends on the number of containers or the size of a bulk lot, as set in the testing rules. With a few containers you sample every container, sometimes more than once; with many containers you sample a set number chosen at random from all positions in the stack. The key principles are:

  1. Take primary samples from the top, middle and bottom of containers and stacks.
  2. Choose containers at random, not only the easy ones on the outside.
  3. Take primary samples of about equal size.
  4. Keep a written record of how many samples you took and from where.

Check as you go

Pour each primary sample onto a clean surface or into a clean container and look at it. If primary samples differ clearly from each other in colour, size, impurities or treatment, stop. Report it to your supervisor; the lot may need to be reprocessed before it can be sampled.

Safety

Seed treated with fungicides or insecticides is a chemical hazard. Read the treatment label, wear the gloves, dust mask and overalls required, do not eat, drink or smoke while sampling, and wash your hands afterwards. Do not lift heavy bags alone; use proper lifting technique or a second person. Never climb unstable stacks.

lessons.title: Reducing, sealing and sending the sample
lessons.html:
From composite sample to laboratory

Mixing and reducing

Combine all primary samples into a composite sample. If it is larger than the submitted sample size required for that crop and those tests, reduce it with an approved method:

  • Mechanical dividers such as a riffle (soil) divider, a conical divider or a centrifugal divider split the sample into equal halves. Pass the seed through repeatedly, keeping one half each time, until you reach the required mass.
  • Modified halving or spoon methods may be used for some crops when the rules allow it.

Never just scoop the top off a bucket. Light seed, chaff and dust tend to rise and heavy seed sinks, so a scoop is not representative.

Packaging

  • Use a clean, strong bag or container. For moisture testing use a moisture-proof, sealed container and fill it so there is little air space.
  • Seal the sample so that it cannot be opened without the seal being broken.
  • Keep a duplicate (reference) sample when your procedure requires it, sealed and stored in cool, dry conditions.

Labelling and documents

Each sample must carry: the lot number, crop and cultivar, seed class, mass of the lot and number of containers, date of sampling, any seed treatment, the tests required (for example germination, purity, moisture, other seed count) and the name and signature of the sampler. Complete the sample submission form and the sampling record. A sample without a lot number is worthless.

Getting it to the laboratory

Send samples promptly. Protect them from heat, rain and direct sun in the bakkie or courier box, because heat and moisture change germination results. Record the dispatch date.

Key points

  • A sample must represent the whole lot, so draw primary samples at random from all positions.
  • Use the right trier or hand method for the seed type and clean tools between lots.
  • Stop and report if primary samples look different from each other.
  • Reduce the composite with an approved divider, never by scooping.
  • Seal, label fully, protect from heat and moisture, and wear PPE for treated seed.
